opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think simplicity bias is a real part of the story, but it's often stated in a way that's a bit too vague to be explanatory. The basic idea is that the parameter-function map of a neural network is highly non-uniform. If you just randomly sample weights, you're vastly more likely to land on functions that are "simple" in some sense — low Kolmogorov complexity, low frequency, whatever measure you prefer — than on complicated ones. And there's good empirical work showing this, like the stuff from Chris Mingard, Ard Louis, and collaborators, where they argue that SGD behaves roughly like a Bayesian sampler from that prior. So you get generalization because the prior already favors functions that tend to match the structure of real-world data.

Where I want to push a bit is on the word "simple." Simple relative to what? There's no universal notion of simplicity that's independent of some reference machine or some choice of features. So when we say networks are biased toward simple functions, what we really mean is that they're biased toward functions that are simple *for that architecture*. And then the substantive claim is that the architecture's notion of simplicity happens to line up with the structure of natural data. That's a much more interesting and contingent claim, and it's not obviously true for every architecture. It's partly why inductive biases like convolution or attention matter so much.

I also think there's a lot of work showing networks learn things in a particular order. They pick up low-order statistics first, like means and covariances, and only later move on to higher-order structure. Some of my own work with colleagues at EleutherAI looked at this distributional simplicity bias: early in training, models behave as if they're only using the first and second moments of the data, and you can actually swap in synthetic data that matches those moments and the early-training behavior barely changes. So simplicity isn't just a static prior over final solutions. It's also a dynamic thing about the trajectory, where the network climbs a kind of ladder of statistical complexity.

So my overall view is that simplicity bias is necessary but not sufficient as an explanation. It tells you why networks don't just memorize in the absence of pressure to do so. But to really understand generalization you need to explain why the network's particular notion of simplicity matches the world, and that pushes you toward thinking about the data distribution itself and how the architecture's symmetries interact with it.

r001.rationale: The response asks “Simple relative to what?” and says there is no universal notion of simplicity, making the explanation depend on how simplicity is defined.

r002.rationale: It calls simplicity bias necessary for explaining generalization and says the architecture’s bias must match the world’s structure, communicating that some inductive bias is required.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, simplicity bias is really the leading candidate explanation we have for why deep learning works at all, and it's worth being precise about what the puzzle is. We have these enormously overparameterized models. Classical learning theory says that if your hypothesis class is big enough to fit random labels, which these networks demonstrably are, you shouldn't expect it to generalize. And yet it does. So something about the training setup has to be picking out the "good" functions from the vast space of functions that all fit the training data equally well.

The simplicity bias story says that the parameter-function map of a neural network is extremely non-uniform. If you just sample random weights, you don't get a uniform distribution over functions. You get a distribution that's heavily concentrated on simple functions, in something like a Kolmogorov complexity sense, or at least in terms of some proxy for it. Chris Mingard and Ard Louis have done nice empirical work on this, showing that the volume of parameter space mapping to a function scales roughly like two to the negative complexity of that function. So there's a kind of Occam's razor baked into the architecture before you've done any training at all.

And then the claim is that stochastic gradient descent, to a first approximation, is sampling from this prior conditioned on fitting the data. It's not doing anything especially clever. It's just that the prior is so skewed toward simple things that the simple interpolating solutions dominate. That lines up with the fact that you can swap out SGD for other optimizers, or even do things closer to random search in small settings, and the generalization behavior is similar. The inductive bias lives primarily in the architecture, not the optimizer.

Where I think it gets more interesting, and where I'd push back a bit on the simplest version of the story, is that "simplicity" is doing a lot of work and it's not a single thing. There's a frequency-domain version, where networks learn low frequency components first and high frequency later. There's a degree-of-polynomial version. There's a version that's about the effective rank or the number of features in use. In some of my own work we found that networks early in training are essentially fitting low-order statistics of the input distribution, like the means and covariances, and only later pick up higher-order structure. So the bias isn't just "simple functions," it's a particular ordering over kinds of structure, and that ordering is what determines what gets learned when.

The other thing I'd say is that the simplicity bias explains why generalization is possible, but it's a double-edged sword for the things I care about, which is alignment and interpretability. A model that's biased toward the simplest explanation of its training data will happily learn spurious shortcuts if they're simpler than the real thing. So the same mechanism that makes these systems work is also what makes them pick up shortcuts and biases from their data. Understanding the exact shape of that bias, which simplicity measure it's actually tracking, feels to me like one of the most important open scientific problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response says simplicity is “not a single thing” and describes several possible measures or forms of simplicity.

r002.rationale: It explains that overparameterized networks need something to select generalizing functions and identifies the architecture’s inductive bias as the primary source.

astra-6.text:
I think simplicity bias is part of the story, but you have to be careful about what you mean by simplicity. A function can be simple in one representation and complicated in another. So the interesting claim isn’t just that neural networks prefer simple functions; it’s that the architecture and training procedure prefer functions that are useful for the kinds of data we actually encounter.

You can have a network that’s expressive enough to memorize arbitrary labels, and yet when you train it on real data, it learns something that generalizes. That tells you expressivity alone isn’t the explanation. You need to understand which solutions training actually finds, among all the solutions that fit the training set.

And simplicity is a plausible way to characterize that preference. But I’d distinguish a descriptive claim—‘the solutions we find tend to have some measure of low complexity’—from an explanation of why those solutions predict unseen examples. For that second step, you also need something about the structure of the world, and how well the network’s biases match it. Otherwise, a preference for simplicity could just make you confidently wrong.

r001.rationale: It says “you have to be careful about what you mean by simplicity” and notes that simplicity depends on representation.

r002.rationale: It says generalization requires understanding which solutions training finds and that explaining predictions on unseen examples also requires the network’s biases to match the structure of the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simplicity bias is part of the story, but you have to be careful about what you mean by simplicity. A neural network can have enough parameters to fit random labels, so the interesting question is why training selects a function that generalizes when you give it real data. The architecture and the optimization procedure impose a preference over the functions it could learn.

But saying that it prefers simple functions doesn’t, by itself, explain why those functions should work on new examples. You also need some relationship between that preference and the structure of the data. A preference for smooth functions is useful when nearby inputs tend to have similar labels; it can be a bad preference when they don’t.

So I’d treat simplicity bias as a hypothesis that needs to be made precise: simple under which representation, according to which measure, and induced by which part of training? Once you specify those things, you can start asking whether the bias actually predicts what the network learns, rather than just calling whatever it learned simple after the fact.

r001.rationale: It says simplicity bias needs to be made precise, asking what counts as simplicity and which measure or representation applies.

r002.rationale: It says architecture and optimization impose a preference over functions, but does not clearly state that neural networks require an inductive bias to generalize.
